workflows.name: YuE2 music cover - re-sing a song in a new style
workflows.description:
Upload a song and get back a cover of it: YuE2 lifts the melody out of your recording as a score, then performs it again as a new piece of music, in whatever style you describe and with whatever lyrics you write.

It is a COVER tool, not a remix - nothing of the original recording survives into the result. What carries over is the tune. So a piano ballad can come back as a brass-band stomp, and it will still be recognisably the same song.

STYLE is the production brief, not a genre word: language, genre, the voice you want, the tempo, and the instruments, e.g. 'English, soulful jazz-pop, expressive male vocal, relaxed 88 BPM, Rhodes piano, upright bass, brushed drums'. The more concrete the instrument list, the closer the arrangement lands.

LYRICS are sung as written, and the section tags matter: mark them [Verse], [Chorus], [Bridge] so the model knows where the song lifts.

WHAT TO FOLLOW: 'melody' takes the tune alone and is the recommended setting for covers; 'full' takes the melody and the chords too, which holds the harmony closer but leaves the arrangement less room to change. The one control sets it for both the transcription and the generation, which have to agree - if they disagree the score is read against the wrong expectation.

LENGTH follows the LYRICS and the extracted score, not the length of the song you uploaded - a 20-second reference with three verses of lyrics produced 98 seconds of music. 'Maximum length' is the ceiling, not the target.

Result: one audio file (FLAC). Licence: YuE2 is a research model - check its terms before any commercial use, and only upload music you have the right to work from.

promptGuides.label: YuE - writing covers (style & lyrics)
promptGuides.tip: Style is a production brief: language, genre, voice, tempo, instruments. Tag lyric sections [Verse] / [Chorus] / [Bridge].

workflows.name: Qwen Image 2.1 — relight a composite (blend an object into a background)
workflows.description:
Harmonise the lighting of a composite. Qwen-Image-2.1 with a community relighting adapter (光影溶图, "light-and-shadow blending"): give it a picture where an object has been dropped onto a background and it re-lights the object to match the scene — key light, specular highlights, front-to-back depth, and the contact shadow that makes something look like it is standing there rather than pasted on.

TWO WAYS TO USE IT, both tested on this rig:

1. ONE picture — put your flat composite in Image 1 and leave the rest empty. This is what the adapter was trained for and it needs no special prompt.

2. TWO pictures — put the BACKGROUND in Image 1 and the object in Image 2, and name them in the prompt: "place the character from <image2> into the scene of <image1>, standing on the path…". ⚠ Both halves of that matter. Put the object in Image 1 and you get the object back on its own white background, because the result always follows Image 1 — and a prompt that never says <image1>/<image2> gives the model nothing to connect.

★ The prompt must start with the trigger word 'pengyu' — without it the adapter is effectively inert. The default is the author's own recommended wording, kept verbatim (including its Chinese punctuation) because that is the phrasing it was trained alongside. Add where the light comes from if it picks the wrong direction.

★ Set 'Relight strength' to 0 for the base model on the same seed with everything else identical — that one field is the whole comparison. Measured here on a cartoon figure pasted onto a dark castle: with the adapter the figure is pulled down to the scene's gloomy key light and the white cut-out fringe at its feet disappears; without it the figure stays brightly lit and still reads as pasted on.

⚠ Trained at about 1 megapixel, so stay near 1 MP. It re-renders rather than compositing pixel-for-pixel, so fine print, faces and logos can change — check them. Experimental: it has not been used in a class yet.

Licence: the adapter is published by RunningHub on behalf of its author with no explicit licence, and the Qwen-Image-2.1 base it runs on is Qwen Research — research and evaluation, not commercial work.

inputs.label: Image 1 — your flat composite, OR (for two pictures) the BACKGROUND. ⚠ The result always follows this picture, so the background belongs here, never the object (<image1>)
Image 2 — the object to place into that background. ⚠ Only used if your prompt names it: “place the object from <image2> into the scene of <image1>…”. Leave empty for a one-picture composite
Image 3 — optional extra reference, e.g. a picture whose lighting to match (<image3>)

workflows.name: Ideogram 4.0 — text to image
workflows.description:
Ideogram 4.0 text-to-image. The prompt must be Ideogram's structured JSON "caption": a high_level_description, a style_description, and a compositional_deconstruction listing the background and each element (objects and text, with a box each). Plain text or JSON in another shape usually comes back as a gray "Image blocked by safety filter" picture, even for harmless subjects.

Click **Compose visually** under the prompt to build the caption without writing JSON: drag boxes on a canvas shaped like your aspect ratio, describe each element, set the style, the background and colors. The line under the prompt says whether the text is in Ideogram's format.

★ **Give every element a box.** Measured on this rig with one harmless prompt over 5 seeds: no box at all was blocked 5/5, one box on the subject 0/5. Adding boxes for the floor, walls or furniture also fills the scene out.

Layout notes, all measured here: boxes are followed closely and placement holds at every aspect ratio and size. Draw each box the shape the thing should be — a tall narrow box makes text read vertically (sometimes upside down). Boxes left apart in empty corners can make Ideogram split the frame into separate panels; keep them adjacent or add floor/wall boxes to hold one scene. In tall formats (9:16, 3:4) elements drift a little towards the middle. Output sizes: 1 MP gives 1024×1024 (1:1), 1376×768 (16:9), 768×1376 (9:16), 896×1184 (3:4), 1568×672 (21:9); 0.25 MP and 2 MP scale that (688×384 and 1936×1088 at 16:9).

Quality presets: Turbo (12 steps, fast) / Default (20) / Quality (48, slow & best).

promptGuides.label: Ideogram 4.0 JSON prompting guide — Ideogram
promptGuides.tip: Fill the JSON: a high_level_description, an optional style_description and a compositional_deconstruction listing every object and text element (the words to render go in their own text element); colors as #RRGGBB.

workflows.name: Krea 2 Turbo — generate in the style of 1–3 pictures
workflows.description:
Generate a new picture in the STYLE of one to three pictures you supply. Krea 2 Turbo reads the look — palette, material, light, brushwork, grain — from your references and applies it to whatever you describe, rather than copying their content.

One reference is enough. A second and third are optional and worth adding when the look is more than one thing at once (say a colour palette from one and a material or texture from another) — they are averaged, so three wildly different pictures give a muddle rather than a blend.

Describe the SUBJECT in the prompt and leave the style to the references: "a white yeti with horns reading a book" plus a reference does more than restating the style in words. Style strength controls how hard the reference pulls: 1.0 is the tested setting, lower it towards 0.6 if the subject is being dragged out of shape.

Enhance prompt with AI rewrites your sentence into a longer one with a local LLM before generating — useful from a few words, unnecessary when you have already written a full description.

promptGuides.label: Krea 2 prompting guide
promptGuides.tip: Describe the subject and the scene; let the reference pictures carry the style. Krea responds well to plain, concrete sentences.

fields.label: Prompt — what to draw (the style comes from the references)
fields.example: a white yeti with horns reading a book that glows

workflows.name: Krea-2 Turbo — text to image (+ style LoRA)
workflows.description:
Fast text-to-image with Krea 2 Turbo (8 steps). Type a prompt, pick an aspect ratio and, if you like, a style LoRA.

"Enhance prompt with AI" lets a small language model rewrite your prompt into a richer description before the image is made; untick it to use your words exactly as written. Keep "Thinking mode" on: with it off, the rewrite sometimes comes back as the AI's working notes, an empty answer or a refusal instead of a description (when ComfyQ can tell, it uses your own words instead).

"Use a style LoRA" applies a trained look (realism is the default). Each style's trigger words are added to the prompt automatically, and while a style LoRA is on the AI rewrite leaves style words out so the LoRA's look is not mixed with another one. Around 1.0 is a good strength; some styles look best near 0.8.

workflows.name: Qwen Image 2.1 - draw from edges (ControlNet canny)
workflows.description:
Upload a picture and the model draws something NEW that keeps its outlines - the shapes and the layout stay, everything else comes from your prompt.

It works from the edges of your picture, so it is at its best where structure is made of clear lines: buildings, objects, vehicles, interiors, a strong silhouette. A hazy or very soft photograph gives it little to hold on to.

Two edge controls decide how much of the picture it traces. Lower "edge detail" finds more lines, including texture you may not want; raise "edge strength" to keep only the confident ones. If the result feels like a tracing, lower the control strength.

The structure picture is scaled to the output size you choose, so pick an aspect ratio close to it or it will be cropped to fit.

Upload up to 16 pictures and refer to them in the prompt as <image1>, <image2> and so on. Image 1 is the one being edited; the rest are references the model can borrow from — a garment, a face, a style, a background. Everything you leave empty is removed from the graph, so an unused slot cannot influence the result.

Upload nothing and it becomes a plain text-to-image generator, and the aspect ratio and size fields decide the output. Upload Image 1 and those two fields are ignored: the result keeps Image 1's size, because any other size shifts the edit.

Say what should STAY as well as what should change — "keep the pose, the face and the background, replace only the jacket" — vague instructions let the model redraw more than you wanted.

workflows.name: Qwen Image 2.1 — text to image
workflows.description:
Make an image from a written description with Qwen Image 2.1. It is unusually good at TEXT inside the picture — signs, posters, packaging, handwriting — in Latin and Chinese alike, so put the words you want rendered in quotes and say where they sit.

workflows.name: Qwen Image 2.1 - with the community "Fix" LoRA
workflows.description:
The same Qwen Image 2.1 text-to-image model as the plain bundle, plus a community adapter that aims to clean up its weak spots - and, just as importantly, the sampling settings its author ships with it.

Built to be compared. Run the plain "Qwen Image 2.1" bundle and this one with the SAME prompt and the SAME seed and look at the two side by side. Easier still: set "Fix strength" to 0 here, which keeps every other setting identical and shows you the same seed without the adapter.

Two things differ from the plain bundle, and it is worth knowing which is which. The adapter itself changes composition noticeably - it tends toward a glossier, shallower-focus photograph. The settings (guidance raised from 1 to 3, a different sampler, and two model patches) are what sharpen detail and fix muddled small print like a watch dial. On the pictures tested here a good part of the improvement came from the settings rather than the adapter, which is exactly what "Fix strength 0" lets you check for yourself.

Guidance above 1 is also why this bundle has a negative prompt at all. At the plain bundle's guidance of 1 a negative prompt does nothing, which is why it does not offer one.

It is MUCH slower: about 46 s against the plain bundle's 14 s on this machine, a bit over 3x. That is arithmetic, not a fault - guidance above 1 makes the model run twice per step, and the seeds_2 sampler is a second-order solver that runs it twice again. Same VRAM (about 15 GB), since the adapter merges into the computation rather than sitting in memory.

You can also tick "Use a start image" and upload a sharp still of the first frame to anchor the result to it; leave it unticked to skip it. Only the start of your clip is used ("Clip length used", default 5 s). This is a fast single 8-step pass.

workflows.name: Unblur & upscale a photo (Qwen Image Edit 2511)
workflows.description:
Sharpen a blurry or low-resolution photograph. Upload a picture and the model re-renders it, recovering detail — it was trained above all to bring back FACES in partly blurred pictures.

Read this before judging it. The adapter's own author says plainly: "This adapter was experimental and trained to recover facial patterns from partially blurred images. The base model produces better overall quality, but it does not preserve those patterns." So it is a trade, not a straight improvement — the adapter holds on to a face's identity, while the model without it may give you a cleaner picture of someone slightly different. Set "Adapter strength" to 0 to see the base model on the same picture and judge for yourself.

This is a RE-RENDER, not an enlarger. The picture comes back at roughly 1 megapixel whatever you put in, so it genuinely enlarges a small or soft picture but will not turn a photo into a poster. For pure enlargement use the PiD upscaler (exactly 4x) or the SeedVR2 upscalers instead.

Because it re-renders, it can also invent: a face can come back subtly changed, and small print or logos can turn to nonsense. Check the result against your original before using it for anything that matters.

Four training checkpoints are installed. The author recommends 20 or 15; 5 and 10 are there so you can see how the effect builds up.

Licence: Apache 2.0 for the adapter — unusually permissive for this family. The Qwen Image Edit base model it runs on is still Qwen Research License (research and evaluation only).

workflows.name: LTX 2.5 IC-LoRA — video to video (canny edges + audio)
workflows.description:
Restyle a video while keeping its outlines and motion. Upload a source video (and, optionally, a start image): the edges of every frame are traced (Canny edge detection) and used as a guide, so LTX 2.5 generates a new video whose shapes, silhouettes and details line up with the original — in the style of your prompt and start image — with a freshly generated soundtrack (the original audio is not kept).

Edges hold on to more of the source's exact shapes and fine lines than the depth version, so this one suits restyles that must stay recognisable (faces, lettering, architecture); the depth version leaves the model more freedom over surfaces and textures. Busy, noisy footage produces busy edges — clean, well-lit shots work best. Strong, physical looks (claymation, toy figures) take hold best; soft painterly styles such as watercolor can stay close to the photographic source.

The start image becomes the opening frame; a restyled still of your video's first frame works best. Untick "Use a start image" to let the prompt alone set the look — then no image is needed. "Enhance prompt with AI" lets a small Gemma model rewrite your prompt into a fuller description first. Lower "Control strength" to let the result drift further from the source's outlines.

Only the start of your clip is used ("Clip length used", default 5 s), at its own frame rate and aspect ratio. The video is rendered in two passes, a fast 8-step pass at the working resolution and then a 2× upscale pass, so a working resolution of 512 gives a 1024p result. Clip length and resolution drive the time.

workflows.name: MiniMax H3 ControlNet (canny) — restyle a video from its outlines + audio
workflows.description:
Upload a video and describe a new look. The clip is turned into an edge map (Canny) and MiniMax H3 generates a brand-new video that follows those outlines — new characters, materials, setting and lighting — with a matching audio track made from your prompt. The original colours and sound are not kept.

Describe the scene, what happens over time, the camera and the sounds (the default prompt shows a good structure with time ranges). "Control strength" sets how tightly the result sticks to the edges. The two edge thresholds decide how much detail is traced: lower keeps faint edges (more detail, but grainy footage gets noisy and flickers), higher keeps only strong contours.

Only the first seconds of your clip are used ("Duration", default 5 s), and the video is centre-cropped to the aspect ratio you pick, so choose the one closest to your clip. Time grows with duration and size; the default 20-step render takes a few minutes, "Fast mode" (4-step turbo LoRA) is several times faster at some cost in quality.

workflows.name: SCAIL-2 (Wan 2.1) — character replacement in video
workflows.description:
Swap the person in a video for your own character. Upload a picture of the character you want to see and a video of someone moving — SCAIL-2 replaces that person with your character, copying their motion while the rest of the scene stays. The built-in segmenter (SAM 3) finds who to replace from the short text you type ("person" works for most clips; be more specific in a crowded scene). The prompt describes the final video: the character's looks, what they do and the setting.

Turn "Replace mode" off to animate your character instead — they perform the video's motion in a scene you describe in the prompt. "Fast mode" (on by default) uses a 6-step distilled LoRA; turning it off runs the full 40-step path, which is many times slower.

It is center-cropped to width × height (896×512 landscape by default — swap the numbers for a portrait clip). Works best with one clearly visible person, framed like the character image.

She holds a large glossy red apple with both hands, using a white paper handkerchief to wipe and clean the apple before smelling and eating it with her eyes closed and a blissful expression. Ripe red and yellow apples hang from leafy branches in the foreground, with rows of green apple trees softly blurred in the background under natural daylight.

workflows.name: Wan Animate 2 — make a character perform a video's motion
workflows.description:
Give your character someone else's moves. Upload a picture of your character (who) and a driving video of a person moving (what motion) — Wan Animate 2 makes your character perform that motion. The motion is read straight from the video frames; no skeleton or pose extraction is needed.

There are two prompts. The Character & background prompt describes how the character looks and where the scene takes place — looks only, no motion words; the background comes from this text, not from your image or the video. The Motion prompt briefly says what the person in the video is doing (e.g. "a man doing an energetic street dance").

Keep the framing similar in both inputs (full body with full body, close-up with close-up) — a framing mismatch is the #1 cause of bad results. Only the first 81 frames of the video are used by default (about 3 s); both inputs are center-cropped to width × height (portrait 480×848 by default — swap the numbers for a landscape clip). Bigger sizes and more frames take longer.

fields.label: Character & background prompt (looks only, no motion)
fields.example:
Character appearance description: A realistic premium collectible action figure of a male street dancer, lifelike matte vinyl and resin material with realistic skin-like paint finish, detailed fabric folds on a black hoodie, dark cargo pants, white sneakers, subtle articulated joints, premium designer toy craftsmanship, standing in a relaxed confident pose facing the camera, full body from head to toe.
Background description: rainy neon-lit city street corner at night, wet asphalt reflecting purple-blue and red neon signs, light mist, cinematic night photography.

fields.label: Motion prompt (what the person in the video does)
fields.example: A man doing energetic street dance with popping body waves and fast spinning moves, rain falling around him.

workflows.name: Wan 2.1 ID-V2V — restyle a video from one keyframe (comparison view)
workflows.description:

Upload your source video and a stylized keyframe — the first frame of that same video, repainted in the look you want (make it with an image-edit workflow such as Flux Klein or Qwen Image-Edit, keeping the same framing). The whole clip is re-rendered in the keyframe's style and lighting. Add a short prompt describing what happens in the clip.

Only the first 81 frames are used (about 3.4 s, read at 24 fps), so trim your video to the moment you want and make sure it is at least that long. The result has no sound.

Width and height MUST match your video's shape, otherwise the picture gets cropped and the style transfer becomes much weaker: square 960×960, landscape 1280×704, portrait 704×1280 — or for a faster test 640×640, 832×480, 480×832. Bigger sizes look cleaner but take longer. Change the seed to re-roll.

This version outputs a comparison video: the restyled result on the right, and a narrower column on the left with your keyframe above the original clip — the quickest way to check the style took and the faces survived (about 1½ minutes at 640×640). For a clean final video, use the "restyle a video from one keyframe" workflow.

workflows.name: FastVideo FastH3 — video with sound, from a first and/or last frame (8 steps)
workflows.description:
Write a scene and get a short film back with its own soundtrack — and optionally pin how it starts, how it ends, or both.

Give a FIRST frame and the clip begins there. Give a LAST frame and it arrives there. Give both and the model travels between them, which is the way to animate between two stills. Give neither and it is plain text-to-video. A slot you leave empty is removed from the graph, so it cannot influence the result.

★ Pick the shape that matches your first frame. The model stretches the first frame to fill the video, so a portrait picture in a widescreen video comes out squashed. The LAST frame is treated differently — it is cropped to fit rather than stretched, so its shape matters less.

Write the prompt the way this model expects: bind the picture to the timeline first, then describe the shot. The default prompt shows the form —
"For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) is fully referenced." followed by "integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] …".

Then describe camera, action and sound in that one block. Naming the audio ("we hear rain on metal, a distant siren") is what earns a deliberate soundtrack rather than an invented one. With no frames at all you can drop the binding line and write the description alone.

This is MiniMax H3 distilled by FastVideo to 8 sampling steps, so it is several times quicker than the full model. Multi-reference conditioning was not distilled — for that use the base MiniMax H3 bundles.

inputs.label: First frame — optional (the clip starts here)
Last frame — optional (the clip ends here)

promptGuides.label: MiniMax H3 — official video prompt guide
promptGuides.tip: Bind the picture to a time first ("at 0.00 seconds … <Picture 1> is fully referenced"), then write one block covering framing, camera move, action and the sound.

promptGuides.label: FastVideo FastH3 8-Step V2 — the distilled checkpoint

fields.label: Prompt — bind the picture to 0.00 s, then the shot, action and sound
fields.example:
For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) is fully referenced.
integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] The camera pushes in slowly as the subject turns towards the lens, natural light, handheld feel. We hear a quiet room tone, fabric movement, and a distant street outside.

choices.label: Shape of the video — match your first frame, it is stretched to fit

limits.label: Steps (8 is what this checkpoint was distilled for)

workflows.name: FastVideo FastH3 — text to video with sound (8 steps)
workflows.description:
Write a scene and get a short film back WITH its soundtrack — dialogue, effects and music are generated together with the picture, in sync.

This is MiniMax H3 distilled to 8 sampling steps by FastVideo, so it is several times quicker than the full model for a small loss of detail.

Describe it like a shot list: camera angle and movement, what is in frame, what happens, and then the sound. The model was trained on descriptions that name the audio explicitly — "we hear footsteps on gravel and distant traffic" earns you that soundtrack; saying nothing about sound gets you whatever it invents.

Duration is in seconds at 24 fps and is snapped to the model’s own frame grid. Keep clips short: cost grows with length and with resolution.

Text to video only. This distilled checkpoint was never trained for first/last-frame conditioning — for that use "MiniMax H3 — first / last frame", which runs the undistilled model.

promptGuides.label: MiniMax H3 — official video prompt guide
promptGuides.tip: Write shot by shot: framing and camera move, subject and action, setting and light — then say what is heard. Naming the audio is what gets you a deliberate soundtrack.

promptGuides.label: FastVideo FastH3 8-Step V2 — the distilled checkpoint

fields.label: Prompt — the shot, the action, and the sound
fields.example: [Shot 1] Cinematic wide shot, slow dolly through a sunlit forest, dust motes drifting in shafts of light, a deer lifts its head and looks into the lens. We hear birdsong, leaves under hoof, and a low warm drone underneath.

limits.label: Steps (8 is what this checkpoint was distilled for)

workflows.name: LTX 2.3 IC-LoRA — image + audio to video (auto-prompt)
workflows.description:
Bring a character image to life with a voice clip. Upload an image and a reference audio (speech), describe the shot, and LTX 2.3 generates a talking video synced to the audio. An in-graph Gemma model rewrites your prompt into an LTX-optimized one (toggle "Enhance prompt with AI" off to use your text as-is).

This is the IC-LoRA / creative variant — it uses the distilled model and no identity LoRA, so it follows your prompt freely rather than locking to a real person's face.

Set the duration to roughly match your audio clip.

promptGuides.label: LTX-2.3 prompt guide — Lightricks blog
promptGuides.tip: Longer, detailed prompts beat short ones: one present-tense paragraph describing the character, their expressions and gestures while they speak, the camera and the setting.

fields.label: Prompt (scene / character / action / camera)
fields.example:
The fuzzy cactus creature is talking to the viewer as it grips the steering wheel with one hand, the other hand gestures naturally as it speaks. The car is moving, revealing the sunlit coastal background, static camera fixed on character, smooth side-tracking shot matching the car speed

scene: Sunlit coastal road trip, clear coastal background
character: Fuzzy cactus creature with big square sunglasses and a Hawaiian shirt
action: One hand grips the steering wheel, the other gestures naturally while talking to the camera
camera: Fixed on character, smooth side-tracking shot matching car speed

fields.label: Negative prompt
fields.example: pc game, console game, video game, cartoon, childish, ugly

workflows.name: LTX 2.3 IC-LoRA — reference sheet to video (ingredients + audio)
workflows.description:
Generate a new video whose characters, props and location match a reference sheet.  The one from Dynamic Charactersheet krea2 for instance or one made by hand.

Upload ONE composite image on a black background with no text, with a clean panel for each element — a face close-up and full-body turnaround for each character, a product-style view of each prop, and one wide shot of the location — then describe what happens. LTX 2.3 with the Ingredients IC-LoRA keeps those elements consistent through the clip and generates matching audio (dialogue written in quotes is spoken).

Write the prompt in two parts, the way the model was trained: first describe the panels on the sheet ("Reference sheet: …"), then the shot, action and sound ("Generated video: …"). Bigger panels carry over better, and anything that isn't on the sheet won't stay consistent.

Duration must be at least 5 seconds (the model needs 121+ frames). The model was trained at 768×448; the 1280×720 default looks sharper but takes longer, and the sheet is letterboxed with black to fit. "Reference strength" controls how strongly the sheet is followed (the model card suggests trying up to 1.4).

inputs.label: Reference sheet (characters / props / location panels on black, no text)

promptGuides.label: LTX-2.3 prompt guide — Lightricks blog
promptGuides.tip: Longer, detailed prompts beat short ones: describe the action and camera over time in one present-tense paragraph, and match the prompt length to the clip length.

fields.label: Prompt (describe the sheet, then the shot / action / dialogue)
fields.example:
### Reference Sheet Description **Top Row Left (Character):** An anthropomorphic bipedal German Shepherd news anchor with realistic brown, tan, and black fur, a calm professional expression, and thin round copper-bronze framed glasses. He is shown in close-up portraits and full-body front, three-quarter, side, and back views standing upright like a person, with a humanoid torso and limbs and a long bushy German Shepherd tail. He wears a vibrant long-sleeve button-down shirt with an abstract multicolored pink-purple-turquoise-yellow woven pattern, dark charcoal dress pants, and dark leather dress shoes. **Top Row Right (Prop):** A professional black studio condenser microphone on a short circular desk stand shown from multiple angles, plus black over-the-ear wireless earpieces / headsets for broadcast cues. **Middle Row Right (Prop):** A flat product view of the same vibrant long-sleeve multicolored patterned button-down shirt, clearly showing the abstract pink, purple, turquoise, and yellow woven texture. **Bottom Row (Setting):** A wide shot of a high-end professional news studio with a large curved dark teal anchor desk in the foreground, a massive digital backdrop screen displaying bold white "NEWS" lettering over soft blue-green abstract graphics, and polished cinematic broadcast lighting with studio fixtures visible around the set.

### Target Description A cozy, cinematic scene inside a high-end professional news studio. The camera begins on a wide establishing shot of the large curved dark teal anchor desk and the soft-focus blue-green "NEWS" backdrop, then smoothly pushes in to a steady medium shot of the anthropomorphic bipedal German Shepherd news anchor seated behind the desk. He has realistic brown-tan-black fur, thin round copper-bronze glasses, and a calm professional expression. He wears the vibrant long-sleeve multicolored pink-purple-turquoise-yellow patterned button-down shirt with dark charcoal dress pants. His paw-like hands rest on the desk near the black studio condenser microphone. The studio is bathed in polished cinematic broadcast light from the backdrop and overhead fixtures. His initial expression is focused and composed, then he leans slightly toward the microphone, softens into a confident on-air smile, and speaks clearly to camera: "Good evening, and welcome to tonight's top stories." He pauses briefly, glances down at the desk, then looks back up and continues: "Here's what you need to know." The background "NEWS" screen and studio lights remain softly detailed behind him, emphasizing his face, glasses, and colorful shirt under the clean broadcast lighting.

workflows.name: LTX 2.5 — first & last frame to video + audio
workflows.description:
Give a START image and an END image and LTX 2.5 generates a short video that travels from the first frame to the last, with a matching audio track. In the prompt, describe what happens in between — the motion, the camera move, and the sounds (e.g. "The hand slowly opens and a glowing crystal appears above the palm; a low hum rises").

Both images are resized and center-cropped to the width × height you choose (1280×720 by default), so use two pictures with the same framing and aspect ratio. Resolution, duration and frame rate drive the generation time far more than anything else.

"Enhance prompt with AI" (off by default) lets a small built-in language model look at the first frame and expand a short prompt into a detailed cinematic one — useful for one-line prompts, but it adds a minute or two.

promptGuides.label: LTX prompting guide — Lightricks
promptGuides.tip: One flowing paragraph in the present tense (4–8 sentences) about what happens: the action in order, the camera movement and the sound, with spoken lines in "quotes". Don't re-describe what is already visible in the image.

fields.label: Prompt (motion + sound)
fields.example: Use the provided start image as the first frame and the provided end image as the final frame anchor. The video opens on the back of the robotic hand, four fingers slightly curled, joints glowing faintly in the darkness, a low electrical hum filling the space. The hand rotates slowly at the wrist, turning from the back view toward the palm side, the four visible fingers uncurling gently one by one, starting with the index finger, then the middle, ring, and pinky, each joint clicking softly. As the palm turns upward, the thumb swings out from the side of the hand into view, clearly separate from the four fingers, all five fingers spreading open. A blue energy crystal fades into existence above the palm, its hum rising into a resonant tone, thin energy threads coiling around it, particles crackling softly as they spiral away like sparks. The crystal rotates slowly, hovering above the fully open hand, light spilling between the five spread fingers, the crystal's steady hum filling the silence as the video ends on the open palm with the glowing crystal.

workflows.name: LTX 2.5 — image to video + audio
workflows.description:
Upload a starting image and describe what happens next — LTX 2.5 animates it into a short video with a matching audio track. In the prompt, describe the action as it unfolds over time, the camera move, and the sounds or dialogue you want to hear (e.g. "She slowly turns her head toward the window as the camera pushes in; rain taps on the glass").

Set the width and height of the video in pixels (multiples of 64) — 1280×704 is a good 16:9 default, 704×1280 a vertical one. Your image is center-cropped to that shape, so match its orientation. Resolution, duration and frame rate drive the generation time far more than anything else, so keep clips short.

"Enhance prompt with AI" (off by default) lets a small built-in language model look at your image and expand a short prompt into a detailed cinematic one — handy for one-line prompts, but it adds a minute or two.

promptGuides.label: LTX prompting guide — Lightricks
promptGuides.tip: One flowing paragraph in the present tense (4–8 sentences) about what happens: the action in order, the camera movement and the sound, with spoken lines in "quotes". Don't re-describe what is already visible in the image.

fields.label: Prompt (motion / camera / sound)
fields.example: Use the provided start image as the first frame. The cybernetic figure slowly turns his head to the right, his glowing blue eyes scanning the horizon, mechanical joints in his neck whirring faintly. The camera follows his gaze, panning across the rooftop to reveal the city beyond: a river of light winding between dark towers, a flying vehicle gliding past between the buildings, its lights streaking. He watches it pass, then his eyes narrow slightly. The camera settles on his profile against the city glow, distant hover traffic humming, wind gusting across the rooftop. No text, no black frames.

limits.label: Width (px, multiple of 64 — your image is center-cropped to this shape)

workflows.name: LTX 2.5 — text to video + audio
workflows.description:
Type a prompt and LTX 2.5 generates a short video from scratch, with a matching audio track — no input image needed. Describe the scene, the action as it unfolds over time, the camera move, and any sounds or dialogue.

Choose an aspect ratio and a resolution in megapixels (0.9 is about 1280×736 in 16:9). Resolution, duration and frame rate drive the generation time far more than anything else, so keep clips short.

"Enhance prompt with AI" (off by default) lets a small built-in language model expand a short prompt into a detailed cinematic one — handy for one-line ideas, but it adds a minute or two.

promptGuides.label: LTX prompting guide — Lightricks
promptGuides.tip: One flowing paragraph in the present tense (4–8 sentences): the shot, the scene and its lighting, the action in order, the characters, the camera movement and the sound. Put spoken lines in "quotes".

fields.label: Prompt (scene / action / camera / sound)
fields.example: A close-up of an Arctic hunter's face, his eyes fixed straight ahead, narrowed and locked on something in the far distance directly in front of him, frost dusting his dark beard, one hand slowly reaching toward the rifle slung on his back, his breath quick and shallow, the tension in his jaw visible even through the scarf. The camera slowly pulls back, revealing him crouched at the edge of an ice floe, and ahead of him, in the exact direction of his gaze, a polar bear moves slowly along a distant ice ridge, its pale coat blending into the white haze, facing toward him. The pull-back continues, the hunter in the foreground and the bear far ahead, the two facing each other across the dark lead of water, the ice field and grey sea stretching around them, seabirds wheeling overhead. Midway through the shot, the complete title "LTX-2.5" fades in large and centered, plain white sans-serif letters with wide spacing, no glow, no shadow, no ornament, the lettering large enough to dominate the center of the frame, emerging slowly from the mist, resting still and blending into the snowscape, with the hunter and the bear still visible below on either side of the title, staying through the end of the scene. The wind carries the distant sound of shifting ice, a single low growl rolling across the water.

workflows.name: MiniMax H3 — image to video + audio (4-step turbo)
workflows.description:
Upload a picture and describe what should happen: your image becomes the first frame and MiniMax H3 animates it into a short video **with a matching audio track**. Describe the motion, the camera move and the sounds you want to hear; you can refer to your image as <Picture 1>.

The video keeps the shape (aspect ratio) of your picture. "Size" sets the resolution: 0.4 megapixels (about 864x480 for a landscape photo) is a good classroom default, 1.0 is close to the 768p the turbo LoRA was trained at and looks better but takes noticeably longer.

"Fast mode" (on by default) uses the 4-step turbo LoRA and is roughly 4x faster than the plain 20-step render. Size and duration drive the cost far more than anything else — time grows roughly with width x height x seconds.

promptGuides.label: MiniMax H3 video prompt guide — MiniMax
promptGuides.tip: Start with the overall style and opening framing, then describe what happens in order. Name camera moves with their speed ("slowly pulls out"), and describe sounds and music concretely — instruments, tempo — rather than moods.

promptGuides.label: H3 prompt tips for ComfyUI — Comfy-Org

fields.label: Prompt (action / camera / sound - refer to the image as <Picture 1>)
fields.example:
The scene from <Picture 1> comes to life. The camera slowly pushes in while the main subject begins to move naturally; light shifts gently and small details in the background drift and sway.
Audio: soft ambient sound that matches the scene, subtle movement sounds, no music.

workflows.name: MiniMax H3 — text to video + audio (4-step turbo)
workflows.description:
Type a prompt and MiniMax H3 generates a short video **with a matching audio track** — no input image needed. Describe the scene, what happens over time, the camera move, and the sounds you want to hear.

This bundle runs the 4-step turbo LoRA, which makes it roughly 4x faster than the plain 20-step path with no other change. Leave "Fast mode" on for classroom use; turn it off if you want the slower, higher-fidelity 20-step render.

Size and length drive the cost far more than anything else — the time grows roughly with width x height x frames. 848x480 at 124 frames (about 5 s at 24 fps) is a good default; 1344x768 is the resolution the turbo LoRA was trained at and looks better, but takes noticeably longer. promptGuides.label: H3 prompt tips for ComfyUI — Comfy-Org

workflows.name: Wan 2.2 — key-frame animation (4 frames to video)
workflows.description:
Turn four still key frames into one continuous video. Wan 2.2 generates a smooth animated transition between each consecutive pair of frames (frame 1→2, 2→3, 3→4) and stitches the three segments into a single clip.

If you are targetting an animation you need to provide a detailled prompt, with context (see the default prompts); leave a box empty to just morph between those two frames. 

 Runs the fast 4-step Lightning path at 720×720.

Tip: use frames that share the same subject and framing so the transitions stay coherent.

fields.label: Motion: key frame 1 → 2 (optional)
fields.example: Red minimalist line art animation of a man performing a capoeira meia lua de compasso. From a standing leaning stance, the man smoothly bends forward at the waist. His torso rotates downward toward the floor as his hands reach down to plant firmly onto the ground for support. His back begins to arch, and his weight shifts entirely onto his hands and pivoting front foot, preparing to unleash the spinning kick. Fluid transition, clean red lines on a plain white background.

fields.label: Motion: key frame 2 → 3 (optional)
fields.example: Red minimalist line art animation of a capoeira spinning kick. With both hands firmly planted on the ground, the man whips his trailing leg upward and outward in a powerful, sweeping horizontal arc. The kicking leg extends fully, cutting through the air in a wide, circular crescent motion. His head looks backward under his arm to track the target. Dynamic motion blur on the sweeping leg, clean red lines on a solid white background.

fields.label: Motion: key frame 3 → 4 (optional)
fields.example: Red minimalist line art animation completing a capoeira movement. The sweeping leg completes its wide circular trajectory, slowing down as it approaches the ground. The man pushes off the floor with his hands, lifting his torso and rotating his upper body back upright. He fluidly transitions out of the inverted position, bringing his feet back underneath him to stand firmly in a defensive capoeira ginga stance from behind. Clean red ink style, seamless transition on a plain white background.
